newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bundesbank's Krupp says not all should join EMU.
newsitem.headline: Bundesbank's Krupp says not all should join EMU.

text.p: Bundesbank member Hans-Juergen Krupp said on Monday not all EU countries could afford to join an EU single currency at the outset, and that it was sensible for them to delay their entry.
Krupp also said all possible preparations had been made to help ensure the single currency would be as stable as the German mark, and that a delay would only lead to fresh complications.
Krupp did not name any EU countries, but said some needed to use the instrument of currency devaluation in order to compensate for inflation which followed from excessive wage increases.
"Countries which do not have cost and wage growth under control cannot afford to join the single currency," he said.
If such countries had not shown they could get inflation under control, there was no reason to assume they would control it better once they joined a single currency, he said.

But Krupp also repeated his often-stated line that the limit of three percent of gross domestic product set for national budget deficits as a qualification criterion for monetary union was an arbitrary one, and less important than control of inflation.
He said the limit had taken little or no account of economic cycles and that it should not be interpreted too strictly to justify a postponement of the planned 1999 start of the single currency.

"A delay would not change the substance of the issue but would make matters much more complicated," he said. "What is the point of waiting until we can achieve 2.9 percent of GDP from a position where the economy is booming?."

Germany has tried to reassure a sceptical public about the stability of a single currency above all by pledging explicitly to keep its budget deficit below 3.0 percent of GDP, and saying that economic convergence must take precedence over the timetable for monetary union.
